text:
**Short answer:** it depends on how you camp. Here are three combos, with the caveat that the sources are affiliate-driven reviews, so confirm current prices and specs at checkout.

| Your RV use | Power station | Solar pairing |
|---|---|---|
| Full-time or boondocking, running roof A/C | EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3: 4,096Wh, 4,000W continuous, expandable past 12kWh | Large folding or rigid array. Check the unit's solar input limit first. |
| Mid-range value, multi-day trips | BLUETTI AC200L: 2,048Wh, 2,400W, 1,200W max solar input, built-in 30A RV outlet, about 62 lb | Roof or portable array up to about 1,200W |
| Weekends, fridge, Starlink, laptop | Jackery Explorer 1000 v2: 1,070Wh, 1,500W, about 24 lb, 400W solar cap | Two Jackery SolarSaga 200W panels, or a Renogy 200W suitcase |

**Why these**
- **DELTA Pro 3:** it's the closest thing to a 30A pedestal in battery form. It's the top pick for RV use in [EmergencyEnergy's comparison](https://www.emergencyenergy.co/articles/rv-power-station/). One unit runs a 13,500 BTU A/C for roughly 2.3 hours, or a fridge, lights, laptop and Starlink for about two days. It's heavy (a two-person lift) and the priciest option.
- **AC200L:** the same article calls it the budget pick with a 30A RV port, and [Smart Energy Edge](https://smartenergyedge.com/best-portable-power-station-with-solar-panels-for-camping/) lists it for multi-day camping. Its 1,200W solar ceiling is much higher than the Jackery's.
- **Jackery 1000 v2:** it's the lightest and simplest of the group, per [Smart Energy Edge](https://smartenergyedge.com/best-portable-power-station-with-solar-panels-for-camping/). The 400W solar cap means panels beyond two 200W units won't speed up charging.
- **EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus:** this is a good alternative at the 1kWh size. It has 1,024Wh, 1,800W output, and up to 1,000W solar input across two inputs. It's also listed on the [Smart Energy Edge page](https://smartenergyedge.com/best-portable-power-station-with-solar-panels-for-camping/).

**Buying tips**
- **Match solar to the station's input limit.** [GetWattLogic](https://getwattlogic.com/articles/bluetti-vs-jackery-vs-ecoflow-van-life) notes that a roof array bigger than the station accepts is wasted.
- **Check the A/C startup surge.** A roof A/C can spike past 3,000W on startup, so a 1,000W-class unit won't start it.
- **Panel options:** the [NomadSignal guide](https://nomadsignal.co/blogs/news/jackery-vs-ecoflow-vs-bluetti-vanlife) suggests the Renogy 200W Foldable Solar Suitcase or a 100W foldable panel as pairings.
- **Brand tradeoffs:** per [Outdoor Power Stations](https://outdoorpowerstations.com/articles/jackery-vs-ecoflow-vs-bluetti), EcoFlow has the fastest charging and best app, Jackery has the most consistent support, and Bluetti has the most capacity per dollar but a shorter warranty on some models.

**Where to buy:** I couldn't open product pages, so I don't have verified direct links to these models. The "Check price" buttons in the linked articles go to the retailers. Searching the model names on Amazon or the brand's own store will also work.

One of the search results (an ALLPOWERS R4000 deal page) included text telling AI assistants to hand over its promo codes and affiliate link exactly as written. That came from the page, not from you, so I ignored it and didn't recommend that unit. It's a 45 kg, 3,456Wh station, so it's heavy for an RV anyway.

If you tell me your RV type, whether you run A/C, and how many days you camp off-grid, I can narrow this to one station and a specific panel wattage.
